title: Cells, Organelles and Membrane Transport
seo_title: Year 11 Biology: Cells and Membranes Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_code: Biology Unit 2: Cells as the basis of life
standard_text: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells; organelles and their functions; measuring cells with microscopes; the fluid mosaic model; diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion, active transport and bulk transport; surface area to volume ratio. (Senior Secondary Biology, Unit 2: Cells and multicellular organisms)
meta_desc: Free Year 11 Biology worksheets on cells: prokaryotes and eukaryotes, organelles, magnification, the fluid mosaic model, diffusion, osmosis, active transport and SA:V ratio. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Convert to the same unit first: 1 mm = 1000 µm.
body_html:
How to think about it

Prokaryotic cells (bacteria, archaea) have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells do. Organelles divide the work: mitochondria release energy, ribosomes make proteins, chloroplasts photosynthesise.

The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins (fluid mosaic model). Substances cross by diffusion, osmosis (water), facilitated diffusion, active transport (needs ATP) and endo- or exocytosis.

As a cell gets bigger its surface area to volume ratio falls, so exchange becomes too slow; that is why cells are small.

Example

An image 30 mm long shows a cell 15 µm long. Magnification?

30 mm = 30 000 µm

30 000 ÷ 15

Answer: ×2000

Example

Cube with 2 cm sides: SA:V?

SA = 6 × 4 = 24 cm²

V = 8 cm³

24 ÷ 8

Answer: 3 : 1

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to convert mm to µm before dividing.
  • Saying water moves by osmosis towards the more dilute solution: it moves to the more concentrated one.
  • Calling active transport ‘diffusion with energy’: it moves substances against the gradient.

faq.q: What is the difference between osmosis and diffusion?
faq.a: Both are passive. Osmosis is the diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane; diffusion can be any particle.

faq.q: Why do large cells have trouble exchanging materials?
faq.a: Volume increases faster than surface area, so each unit of volume has less membrane for exchange.

items.q: Why is cell fractionation done in an ice-cold, isotonic, buffered solution?
c: to stop enzymes working, stop osmosis damaging organelles and keep pH constant
items.e: Then the homogenate is filtered and centrifuged.

items.q: A mitochondrion is 2.50 µm long. Its image is 12.5 mm long. Calculate the magnification.
items.e: Change mm to µm: 12500 µm. Magnification = image ÷ actual = ×5000.

items.q: Which structure is found in plant cells but not animal cells?
items.e: Plant cells also have chloroplasts and a large vacuole.

items.q: What are the ribosomes of prokaryotes?
items.e: Mitochondria and chloroplasts also have 70S ribosomes.

items.q: What is the main function of ribosomes?
c: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia
items.e: Ribosomes: the site of protein synthesis.

items.q: Why is cancer linked to uncontrolled mitosis?
c: mutations in genes that control the cell cycle
items.e: Tumours form from rapidly dividing cells.

items.q: In ultracentrifugation, which organelle forms the first pellet?
items.e: The heaviest organelles settle at the lowest speed.

items.q: What happens in interphase?
c: DNA replicates and the cell grows
chromosomes line up at the equator
items.e: Organelles are also copied.

items.q: What do lysosomes contain?
items.e: They digest worn-out organelles and pathogens.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for storing water, sap and waste, and keeping the cell turgid?
items.e: Vacuole: storing water, sap and waste, and keeping the cell turgid.

items.q: Why can oxygen diffuse straight through the phospholipid bilayer?
items.e: Ions need channel proteins.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for the site of protein synthesis?
items.e: Ribosomes: the site of protein synthesis.

items.q: What is the main function of Golgi apparatus?
c: packaging and secretion of materials, and forming glycoproteins and glycolipids
giving colour to fruits and flowers
storing water, sap and waste, and keeping the cell turgid
items.e: Golgi apparatus: packaging and secretion of materials, and forming glycoproteins and glycolipids.

items.q: What is the function of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
items.e: It has no ribosomes.

items.q: A plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution. What happens?
c: water leaves and the cell becomes plasmolysed
water enters and the cell bursts
the cell takes in salt by osmosis
items.e: The membrane pulls away from the cell wall.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for making ribosomal RNA?
items.e: Nucleolus: making ribosomal RNA.

items.q: Why must cells stay small?
c: as a cell grows, its surface area to volume ratio falls, so exchange becomes too slow
items.e: Volume grows faster than surface area.

items.q: What happens in metaphase of mitosis?
c: chromosomes line up at the equator, attached to spindle fibres
items.e: Spindle fibres attach to centromeres.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for making lipids and steroid hormones?
items.e: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum: making lipids and steroid hormones.

items.q: What is the main function of chloroplasts?
c: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia
packaging and secretion of materials, and forming glycoproteins and glycolipids
items.e: Chloroplasts: photosynthesis.

items.q: Which organelles contain their own DNA and ribosomes?
items.e: They are semi-autonomous.

items.q: In a photograph a nucleus is 100 mm long. The magnification is ×20000. Calculate its actual length in µm.
items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 100 mm ÷ 20000 = 0.00500 mm = 5.00 µm.

items.q: What is the main function of nucleolus?
c: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia
items.e: Nucleolus: making ribosomal RNA.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for packaging and secretion of materials, and forming glycoproteins and glycolipids?
items.e: Golgi apparatus: packaging and secretion of materials, and forming glycoproteins and glycolipids.

items.q: What is the space between the two layers of the nuclear envelope called?
items.e: The envelope has nuclear pores.

items.q: Which ribosomes are found in prokaryotes?
items.e: Eukaryotes have 80S in the cytoplasm.

items.q: A yeast cell is 8.00 µm long. How long will its image be, in mm, at a magnification of ×4000?
items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 32000 µm = 32.0 mm.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for making and secreting proteins?
items.e: Rough endoplasmic reticulum: making and secreting proteins.

items.q: In a photograph a cheek cell is 10.0 mm long. The magnification is ×200. Calculate its actual length in µm.
items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 10.0 mm ÷ 200 = 0.0500 mm = 50.0 µm.

items.q: What is the folded inner membrane of mitochondria called?
items.e: They increase the surface area.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)?
items.e: Mitochondria: the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell).

items.q: What is the main function of lysosomes?
c: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia
packaging and secretion of materials, and forming glycoproteins and glycolipids
items.e: Lysosomes: digesting materials with hydrolytic enzymes.

items.q: What is the main function of leucoplasts?
c: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia
items.e: Leucoplasts: storing starch, oils and proteins.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for giving colour to fruits and flowers?
items.e: Chromoplasts: giving colour to fruits and flowers.

items.q: Who first saw and described a living cell?
items.e: Hooke saw dead cork cells.

items.q: Which part of the cell is the largest cell in the human body?
items.e: The longest cell is the nerve cell.

items.q: What is the cell wall of plants mainly made of?
items.e: Fungal walls are mainly chitin.

items.q: What is the main function of chromoplasts?
c: giving colour to fruits and flowers
forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia
items.e: Chromoplasts: giving colour to fruits and flowers.

items.q: Who discovered the nucleus?
Which organelles are called suicidal bags?
items.e: Their enzymes can digest the cell itself.

items.e: Change mm to µm: 5000 µm. Magnification = image ÷ actual = ×100.

items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 50000 µm = 50.0 mm.

items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 80.0 mm ÷ 20000 = 0.00400 mm = 4.00 µm.

A pollen grain is 50.0 µm long. How long will its image be, in mm, at a magnification of ×5000?

items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 20000 µm = 20.0 mm.

items.e: Change mm to µm: 200000 µm. Magnification = image ÷ actual = ×5000.

items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 20000 µm = 20.0 mm.

items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 12500 µm = 12.5 mm.

items.q: In a photograph a palisade cell is 20.0 mm long. The magnification is ×200. Calculate its actual length in µm.
items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 20.0 mm ÷ 200 = 0.100 mm = 100 µm.

items.q: In a photograph a palisade cell is 10.0 mm long. The magnification is ×200. Calculate its actual length in µm.
items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 10.0 mm ÷ 200 = 0.0500 mm = 50.0 µm.

items.q: A guard cell is 25.0 µm long. Its image is 100 mm long. Calculate the magnification.
items.e: Change mm to µm: 100000 µm. Magnification = image ÷ actual = ×4000.

items.q: A guard cell is 25.0 µm long. How long will its image be, in mm, at a magnification of ×10000?
items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 250000 µm = 250 mm.

items.q: In a photograph a guard cell is 100 mm long. The magnification is ×4000. Calculate its actual length in µm.
items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 100 mm ÷ 4000 = 0.0250 mm = 25.0 µm.

items.q: In a photograph a cheek cell is 75.0 mm long. The magnification is ×1500. Calculate its actual length in µm.
items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 75.0 mm ÷ 1500 = 0.0500 mm = 50.0 µm.

items.q: In a photograph a yeast cell is 25.0 mm long. The magnification is ×5000. Calculate its actual length in µm.
items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 25.0 mm ÷ 5000 = 0.00500 mm = 5.00 µm.

items.q: A pollen grain is 25.0 µm long. Its image is 250 mm long. Calculate the magnification.
items.e: Change mm to µm: 250000 µm. Magnification = image ÷ actual = ×10000.

items.q: Cell A has a water potential of −300 kPa and cell B has −200 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−200 kPa) is higher.

items.q: Which process moves large particles out of a cell in vesicles?
items.e: Vesicles fuse with the membrane to release their contents.

items.q: What is the fluid mosaic model?
c: a phospholipid bilayer with proteins that can move within it
a layer of DNA around the cell
items.e: Proteins float in a fluid bilayer.

items.q: Cell X has a water potential of −1200 kPa and cell Y has −1000 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from cell Y to cell X
from cell X to cell Y
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: A potato cell has a water potential of −150 kPa and the sucrose solution has −600 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−150 kPa) is higher.

items.q: What is osmosis?
c: movement of any particle from high to low concentration
net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute to a more concentrated solution
movement of salt across a membrane
items.e: Water moves towards the higher solute concentration.

items.q: What is facilitated diffusion?
c: passive movement through channel or carrier proteins
items.e: Glucose and ions often need protein channels.

items.q: What is active transport?
c: movement down a gradient with no energy
movement against a concentration gradient using carrier proteins and ATP
items.e: Root hair cells take up mineral ions this way.

items.q: Cell A has a water potential of −400 kPa and cell B has −350 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from cell A to cell B
from cell B to cell A
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: A potato cell has a water potential of −200 kPa and the sucrose solution has −700 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from a potato cell to the sucrose solution
from the sucrose solution to a potato cell
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: Why is a virus not considered a living cell?
c: it has no cytoplasm or ribosomes and can only replicate inside a host cell
items.e: Viruses are acellular.

items.q: What is the cell wall of a bacterium made of?
items.e: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose.

items.q: A red blood cell is placed in pure water. What happens?
c: the cell wall stops it bursting
water leaves and the cell shrinks
water enters by osmosis and the cell may burst
items.e: Animal cells have no cell wall.

items.q: Cell X has a water potential of −700 kPa and cell Y has −800 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−700 kPa) is higher.

items.q: Cell A has a water potential of −400 kPa and cell B has −700 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−400 kPa) is higher.

items.q: Why do phospholipids form a bilayer in water?
c: their phosphate heads are hydrophilic and their fatty acid tails are hydrophobic
items.e: Tails face inwards away from water.

items.q: An onion cell has a water potential of −700 kPa and the salt solution has −400 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from the salt solution to an onion cell
from an onion cell to the salt solution
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: How does a white blood cell take in a bacterium?
items.e: The membrane surrounds the particle.

items.q: Which microscope has the highest resolution?
items.e: Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light.

items.q: Which factor increases the rate of diffusion?
items.e: Fick's law: rate ∝ area × difference ÷ thickness.

items.q: How are monoglycerides and fatty acids absorbed into ileum cells?
c: micelles carry them to the cell, then they diffuse through the membrane
items.e: In the cell they reform triglycerides and form chylomicrons.

items.q: How is air carried to the cells of an insect?
items.e: Gas exchange happens at the tracheole ends.

items.q: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 10 cm, as x : 1.
What is the evidence that mitochondria were once free-living bacteria?
c: they have their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and a double membrane
they are found in every prokaryote
they are bigger than the nucleus
items.e: This is the endosymbiotic theory.

items.q: What is diffusion?
c: movement against a concentration gradient using ATP
net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration
movement of large particles in vesicles
items.e: Diffusion is passive.

items.q: A block of agar is 2 cm × 4 cm × 8 cm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio, as x : 1.
Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 3 cm, as x : 1.
Why are alveoli efficient gas exchange surfaces?
c: a large surface area, thin walls and a good blood supply
items.e: Ventilation keeps a steep gradient.

items.q: Which statement compares prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells correctly?
c: only eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
items.e: Both have a membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA.

items.q: How do xerophytes reduce water loss?
c: more stomata on the upper surface
sunken stomata, rolled leaves and hairs that trap moist air
items.e: These reduce the water potential gradient.

items.q: Why do single-celled organisms not need a gas exchange system?
c: they have a large surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion is fast enough
items.e: Larger organisms need specialised surfaces.

items.q: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 8 cm, as x : 1.
A block of agar is 1 cm × 4 cm × 5 cm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio, as x : 1.
What is the counter-current system in fish gills?
c: water and blood flow in opposite directions, keeping a diffusion gradient along the whole lamella
blood flows back into the mouth
water and blood flow the same way
items.e: More oxygen is absorbed than with parallel flow.

items.q: What happens during inspiration?
c: the external intercostal muscles and diaphragm contract, so the volume of the thorax increases
items.e: Air pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure.

items.q: Which molecule can diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer?
items.e: Small, non-polar molecules pass easily.

items.q: How does asthma reduce the rate of gas exchange?
c: the airways narrow, so less air reaches the alveoli
items.e: Inflamed bronchioles produce mucus.

items.q: What do bile salts do in digestion?
items.e: This gives lipase a larger surface area.
